context_blurb:
Coiled inside nearly every cell of your body is a set of instructions for building you, written in DNA, and half of it came from each parent. Small changes in it, called mutations, can cause a deadly blood disease that also guards against malaria, or give the world a new fruit.

DNA is packed into chromosomes, thread-like bundles in the cell's nucleus, its control centre. A gene is a section of that DNA holding the instructions for one working part of the body, often a protein. Virtually every cell holds a complete copy of a person's genes in its nucleus, so cells scraped from inside a girl's cheek hold her eye-colour genes, though only her irises use them.

In 1902 at Columbia University, the graduate student Walter Sutton watched a grasshopper's chromosomes. Nearly all were matched pairs whose partners split up, one into each sex cell, a cell that passes to the young, just as Mendel's paired factors for a trait do. So the factors, later named genes, must ride on chromosomes, and since an animal has far more traits than chromosomes, Sutton proposed in 1903 that each chromosome carries many genes. A human chromosome holds hundreds to thousands.

Theophilus Painter's count of 48, made in the early 1920s from clumped, overlapping chromosomes, stood for some thirty years. In December 1955, at Lund in Albert Levan's laboratory, Joe Hin Tjio studied human cells grown in culture, supplied by Rune Grubb. He halted them mid-division with the drug colchicine, swelled them in weakly salted water and pressed them flat, so each chromosome lay apart. Almost every whole cell held 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs: 22 matched pairs plus one pair of sex chromosomes.

Photograph one cell's chromosomes and sort them into look-alike pairs, and you have a karyotype. Each pair holds one chromosome from the mother and one from the father, so a person carries two copies of nearly every gene. Partners carry the same genes, in versions that can differ. Each parent passes on one copy of each gene, chosen by chance, so each child gets a different half of each parent's genes. That is why sisters can look unlike: full sisters share only about half their DNA, and only identical twins share all of it.

In 1905 Nettie Stevens counted a mealworm's chromosomes: a female's cells held 20 large ones, a male's 19 large and one small. Many biologists thought surroundings settled sex, but Stevens showed that it follows the chromosomes. Human females are XX and males XY. A mother gives every child an X; a father carries an X and a Y and passes on one or the other, his X to every daughter and his Y to every son, so the father's chromosome decides.

A mutation is a lasting change in a gene, from copying mistakes, radiation or some chemicals; most harm or do nothing, and a few help. In Austin, Texas, in 1926, Hermann Muller blasted fruit flies with X-rays and bred them beside untreated flies. The X-rayed flies' young showed new inherited changes far more often: about 150 times as many deadly mutations. The rays had reached the cells that make the next generation, and in 1946 Muller won a Nobel Prize for showing that radiation can change genes.

In 1910 James Herrick of Chicago described the sickle-shaped red cells that his intern Ernest Irons had seen in a Grenadian dental student's blood. The cause is one small change in a single gene, a gene for haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. A child with two changed copies has the disease; where care is poor, half or more such children die before turning five.

Yet in the early 1950s Anthony Allison found that over one in five people on malaria-ridden coasts of East Africa carried the gene. A child with one copy has the sickle-cell trait, usually with no illness, and survives malaria far better, with fewer malaria parasites in the blood. Where malaria kills many children, carriers live to pass the gene on, so it stays common. Malaria never makes the gene; it only decides who lives to pass it on.

Not every mutation harms. A nectarine is a smooth-skinned peach, of the same species. Its smooth skin comes from a change in one gene that peach fuzz needs, and every nectarine traces back to a single mutation long ago. The belief that a nectarine is a peach crossed with a plum is a myth.
